screens.title: Data Model Design for URLs and Pastes
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to design practical data models for two common services: a URL shortener and a Pastebin. We'll define the fields you must store, pick appropriate data types, and reason about which database style makes sense given the access pattern. You will see concrete S Q L table definitions for both services, and we will contrast those with NoSQL and object storage approaches. This matters because good data design makes retrieval fast, storage efficient, and growth predictable. For example, a redirect request depends on a single fast lookup by short code, while paste retrieval may involve very large content blobs that are expensive to keep inside a relational row. We'll also cover indexing strategies, common mistakes like not planning for access patterns, and secure handling of private data such as password hashes. By the end you should be able to choose a primary key, pick sensible types, and recommend when to cache, index, or offload content. Keep in mind the core idea: model data around how it will be read and updated at scale.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Overview
Data Model Design for URLs and Pastes
Learn why field selection, types, indexes, and storage choices shape performance and cost.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

We’ll map the short code to a real URL, design a paste document that can include megabytes of text, and decide when to use SQL, NoSQL or object storage. Expect concrete schemas, indexing rules, and common mistakes to avoid.

ShortenedURL
Primary key: short_code. High-volume reads. Candidate for key-value cache.
Paste
Content may be large. Consider document store or object storage for blobs.
Indexing
Index short keys and frequently queried metadata like active expires_at.
Security
Never store plain passwords; use a strong hash for private pastes.
Coming up

Fields, PK, indexing for low-latency redirects.
Paste model
Handling large content and access control.
SQL vs NoSQL
When to prefer consistency or scale and flexibility.
Visual Concept
Short code → original URL
Extremely frequent read. Ideal for key-value caching.
Paste document
Variable size content. Consider external object storage for large blobs.
Connections
Use a relational store for metadata and a cache or object storage for heavy or hot data.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to design data schemas for both a URL shortener and a Pastebin service. That means selecting primary keys, choosing field types for variable-length data, and deciding what should be nullable. You will also identify which database model — relational or non-relational — matches a given access pattern. For example, when redirect latency matters and lookups are simple key-to-value, a key-value store or a cached mapping is often the best fit. When paste contents vary greatly in size, a document store or object storage reference is preferable. You will also assess indexing strategies: which columns must be indexed to support fast queries and which can remain unindexed to reduce overhead. Finally, you will identify security constraints such as storing password hashes rather than plaintext, and plan for growth by choosing fields and indexes that scale. These skills let you build efficient, maintainable storage for both services.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied
screens.narratorSegment: Now let’s translate objectives into actions you can perform in an interview or design doc. First, define the ShortenedURL table with a primary key short_code and choose a type that supports six to eight alphanumeric characters. Second, specify the Paste schema and decide whether content stays in the database or files are stored in object storage. Third, design indexes that make the common queries fast — for example, a primary key index on short_code and a filtered index on non-null expires_at for cleanup tasks. Fourth, propose a hybrid storage plan: use a relational database for metadata, a key-value cache for hot redirect lookups, and object storage for very large paste content. Each of these actions shows you understand the trade-offs between consistency, latency, and cost. Practice explaining the rationale: when you prefer ACID transactions and when you prefer horizontal scalability. This applied perspective helps you defend your choices during a system design interview.

screens.title: ShortenedURL — Core Fields
screens.narratorSegment: A ShortenedURL entity maps a short_code to an original_url and carries metadata used by the service. The short_code must be unique and indexed because redirects are high-volume lookups. Use a VARCHAR sized for six to eight alphanumeric characters to keep keys compact. The original_url should be a TEXT or a large VARCHAR so very long destinations are supported. created_at and expires_at timestamps let you audit and expire entries. A user_id links a short URL to its owner when user accounts exist; treat that as nullable if anonymous creation is allowed. click_count is an often-updated counter and can be stored as a big integer; for very high write rates consider incrementing in a cache and persisting periodically. status as an ENUM helps manage states like active, expired, or disabled. One common misconception is to treat all fields the same: hot key fields like short_code need tight indexing and fast reads, while metadata can be updated less aggressively. Example: when a redirect arrives you only need short_code to original_url; avoid fetching large user metadata during that path. Takeaway: model fields around their runtime use and rate of access.

keyIdea.title: Design Principle
keyIdea.text: Separate the hot lookup key and minimal redirect data from less frequently used metadata to optimize latency.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › ShortenedURL Fields
Definition
ShortenedURL is the primary entity mapping short_code to original_url with metadata for management and analytics.
Core fields
  • short_code — primary key, indexed for fast redirect.
  • original_url — TEXT or large VARCHAR for long targets.
  • created_at / expires_at — timestamps for auditing and cleanup.
  • user_id — nullable FK if users exist.
  • click_count — big integer for counts; consider eventual persistence from cache.
  • status — ENUM to manage state.
Common mistake
Treating click_count as a transactional hot column without considering write amplification and contention at high scale.
Key Takeaway

Keep the redirect path minimal: short_code and original_url must be optimized for the fastest possible lookup.

Example SQL schema
CREATE TABLE shortened_urls (    short_code VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,    original_url TEXT NOT NULL,    created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,    expires_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NULL,    user_id UUID NULL,    click_count BIGINT DEFAULT 0,    status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'active'    -- INDEXES OMITTED FOR BREVITY);
Concrete scenario: a redirect request looks up short_code. If short_code is in a cache, the redirect will be millisecond-level. If you stored extra joins in that path, latency increases.
Check your understanding
Why would you make user_id nullable? Because some short URLs are created anonymously and should still be resolvable without a user record.

screens.title: Access Patterns for a URL Shortener
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding access patterns is the practical heart of data model design. For a URL shortener the write path is usually: generate a short_code and insert a new record with original_url and metadata. Reads are extremely frequent: each redirect needs a fast lookup by short_code. Updates are common for click_count increments and occasional status changes. Deletes happen in batch for expired or disabled URLs. Because reads vastly outnumber writes, prioritize read latency: make the short_code lookup as cheap as possible by using a primary key index or a key-value cache. A typical optimization is to store short_code → original_url in a key-value store like Redis for the redirect service and persist metadata to a relational database asynchronously. A misconception is to over-index every column; that can slow writes and inflate storage. Example: only index user_id if you support queries like "list my short URLs." For cleanup, a partial index on expires_at where expires_at IS NOT NULL AND status = 'active' helps the background job find candidates quickly. Question: if read volume spikes, which layer should you scale first — cache or primary store?

keyIdea.title: Access Pattern Rule
keyIdea.text: Design indexes and caches based on the dominant operation: in shorteners, optimize for fast reads by key and offload metadata updates.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Access Patterns
Access Pattern: Redirect service
A short sequence of actions shows different performance needs.
Write
Insert short_code + original_url.
Read (hot)
Lookup original_url by short_code at high QPS.
Update
Increment click_count or change status.
Delete
Batch remove expired/disabled entries.
Optimization pattern
  • Cache hot short_code → original_url mapping in a key-value store.
  • Persist metadata and audit trails in a reliable SQL store.
Misconception
Indexing every metadata column will slow writes and increase storage; index only what you query frequently.
Key Takeaway

Favor read-optimized lookups and cache hot keys. Use partial indexes to speed maintenance queries.

screens.title: Paste — Core Fields and Security
screens.narratorSegment: A Paste entity stores textual content along with metadata that controls access and lifecycle. Core fields include paste_id as a unique identifier and content as a TEXT or BLOB depending on variability. syntax_highlighting_language is optional but useful for rendering. created_at and expires_at manage lifecycle. access_control distinguishes public, unlisted, and private pastes. If private pastes require a password, never store it in plain text; store a password_hash produced by a strong hashing algorithm such as bcrypt. user_id links pastes to accounts when applicable. view_count tracks reads and can be incremented similarly to click_count. A common mistake is to keep raw passwords or to place very large content directly into transactional hot tables without considering performance. Example: a 5 MB paste stored as a TEXT column can bloat backups and slow queries. Consider storing only metadata in the database and the content in object storage, with a reference in the record. This keeps the metadata fast to scan and the large data in a service designed for big objects. Paste — Core Fields and Security means keep sensitive authentication material hashed and consider external storage for large content to preserve database performance.. In practical terms, essential metadata, content handling, and protecting private pastes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Paste Fields
Paste entity: fields and protection
Model content size and access rules up front to avoid scalability and security problems.
Core fields
  • paste_id — primary key for retrieval.
  • content — TEXT or store externally if large.
  • syntax_highlighting_language — optional rendering hint.
  • access_control — public, unlisted, private.
  • password_hash — store hashed password if private.
  • view_count — track views.
Security note
Never store plain passwords. Use a strong password hashing algorithm. Keep access control checks at read time before returning content.
Example scenario
When a user requests a private paste, verify the password by comparing the provided secret against the stored hash. Only after successful verification should the system fetch the content, whether from DB or object storage.
Key Takeaway

Treat content size and access control as first-class design concerns; secure credentials with hashing and plan storage accordingly.

screens.title: Example SQL Schema for Pastebin
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a practical S Q L schema that captures the paste metadata while leaving options for content storage. The paste_id is the primary key for fast lookup. content is declared as TEXT, which is acceptable for moderate sizes, but if you expect megabyte-level pastes you should consider object storage and store a reference instead. We include syntax_highlighting_language, created_at, expires_at, access_control, password_hash, user_id, and view_count. Indexes include user_id when you need to query a user's pastes and a conditional index on expires_at to accelerate cleanup jobs. An important misconception to avoid is assuming that indexing expires_at unconditionally will always help; indexing only active expiration values reduces index bloat. Concrete example: a cleanup job that finds all active pastes with expires_at < now will benefit from a partial index on expires_at where expires_at IS NOT NULL. When explaining this schema in an interview, highlight how each index supports an access pattern and how content storage decisions reduce operational overhead. Example SQL Schema for Pastebin means use a metadata-first sql table and consider partial indexes for lifecycle queries; offload content when sizes grow large.. In practical terms, a concrete table definition and index hints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Paste SQL
SQL definition (example)
CREATE TABLE pastes (  paste_id VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY,  content TEXT NOT NULL,  syntax_highlighting_language VARCHAR(50) NULL,  created_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,  expires_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NULL,  access_control VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'public',  password_hash VARCHAR(255) NULL,  user_id UUID NULL,  view_count BIGINT DEFAULT 0  -- INDEXES:  -- INDEX idx_user_id (user_id),  -- INDEX idx_expires_at (expires_at) WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL;
Indexing hints
  • Primary key on paste_id for direct retrieval.
  • Index user_id only if you plan listing by owner.
  • Use partial index on expires_at to limit index size and speed cleanup.
Example: a cleanup query looking for expired active pastes will scan the partial index instead of the whole table.

screens.title: SQL vs NoSQL: URL Shortener
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between S Q L and NoSQL depends on your requirements. For a URL shortener a relational database gives you strong consistency, transactional guarantees, and easy joins if you link URLs to users or billing records. It is a good fit when you need complex queries or strong integrity. A NoSQL key-value store, however, excels at the main redirect path: an extremely fast lookup by short_code with horizontal scalability and low latency. Many teams use a hybrid approach: store authoritative metadata in S Q L for correctness and auditability, while using a key-value cache for the redirect hot path. A common misconception is that NoSQL always means weaker correctness; actually, many NoSQL systems offer tunable consistency and can be perfectly safe when you design around eventual consistency. Example: place short_code → original_url pairs into Redis with a TTL for hot entries and persist authoritative rows to PostgreSQL. In an interview, explain the trade-offs and justify caching based on read volume and latency needs. SQL vs NoSQL: URL Shortener means use sql for integrity and complex queries; use nosql key-value for extremely low-latency hot lookups; hybrid solutions combine strengths.. In practical terms, when to prefer a key-value store or a relational table. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › SQL vs NoSQL
SQL vs NoSQL for shorteners
Compare capabilities and pick based on performance, consistency, and query complexity.
Relational (SQL)
  • ACID transactions and strong integrity.
  • Good for joins, analytics, and complex queries.
NoSQL (Key-value)
  • Extremely fast lookup, horizontal scale, low latency.
  • Ideal for hot redirect cache.
Practical hybrid
Persist authoritative ShortenedURL rows in SQL. Cache frequently accessed short_code entries in Redis or DynamoDB. Keep consistency boundaries clear: cache misses read from SQL and refresh cache.
Key Takeaway

Articulate why you chose SQL, NoSQL, or both and tie each choice to a concrete access pattern.

screens.title: Access Patterns for Pastebin
screens.narratorSegment: Pastebin has different load characteristics from a URL shortener. Writes create potentially large documents at insert time. Reads fetch content and metadata by paste_id. Updates are usually limited to view_count increments or metadata changes. Deletes happen for expired pastes. Because content size varies widely, the main design question is where to store content: inside the database as TEXT or externally in object storage. If you store in the DB, large content increases row size and can slow scans, backups, and memory usage. If you offload content, the database stores a lightweight reference and metadata; the application fetches the object storage content when needed. A misconception is thinking object storage introduces unacceptable latency — in practice, object stores are optimized for large payloads and can be cached at the CDN layer. Concrete example: store a 10 MB paste in object storage and keep paste_id, access_control, and password_hash in the DB. Takeaway: align content location with expected size distribution and read latency needs. Access Patterns for Pastebin means store metadata in db; offload large or infrequent content to object storage to preserve db performance.. In practical terms, writes, reads, updates, and content lifecycle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.3 › Paste Access Patterns
Pastebin access pattern
Decide storage based on the size-frequency distribution of paste content.
Write
Insert metadata and content or content pointer.
Read
Fetch metadata and then content from DB or object storage.
Update
Increment view_count or change access_control.
When to use object storage
Content larger than a few hundred KB or when you want to reduce DB backup size and memory pressure.
Misconception
Assuming DB storage is simpler but failing to account for backup and read costs for large binaries.
Key Takeaway

Choose object storage for large blobs; keep metadata in DB to preserve query performance and reduce operational load.

screens.title: Hybrid Architecture: Cache, DB, and Object Storage
screens.narratorSegment: A hybrid architecture often gives the best balance between performance and correctness. For the redirect service, keep an authoritative S Q L or NoSQL store for durability and auditing, and layer a key-value cache to answer most redirect requests with minimal latency. For Pastebin, keep metadata in the database and place large content in object storage; use a CDN for frequently accessed large pastes. The pattern is: cache for low-latency reads, database for authoritative metadata and transactions, and object storage for heavy payloads. An important misconception is thinking caches replace databases — they don't. Caches are ephemeral and must be refreshed from the authoritative store on miss. Example deployment: client requests a short URL; the redirect service checks Redis; on miss it reads PostgreSQL, returns the URL, and populates Redis. For pastes, the app reads DB metadata, then fetches content from object storage using the stored reference or serves from CDN. When explaining this in an interview, show how each layer handles different SLAs and failure modes. In practical terms, combining persistence and performance for both services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Pitfalls in Data Model Design
screens.narratorSegment: Many design mistakes come from not aligning schema choices with access patterns. First, not indexing the short_code is a fatal error for a redirect service: it makes every redirect scan the table. Second, over-normalization can cause excessive joins and hurt latency; under-normalization can cause redundancy and update anomalies. Strike a balance based on expected queries. Third, storing plaintext passwords for private pastes is a security vulnerability; always store a strong hash. Fourth, putting very large content inside transactional tables without offloading to object storage will bloat backups and increase memory pressure. Fifth, indexing every column without thought increases write latency and storage. Example: adding an index on a rarely queried metadata column creates write overhead for every insert. When you describe your design, be explicit about why you indexed specific columns and how that supports a concrete access pattern. Finally, plan for growth: choose flexible types and avoid fixed-size VARCHAR that may overflow in the future. Pitfalls in Data Model Design means index hot keys, hash secrets, avoid ill-considered indexes, and offload large blobs to appropriate storage to prevent operational pain.. In practical terms, mistakes to avoid when modeling url and paste data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Indexing Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Indexing is key to query performance, but indexes also carry cost. Primary keys on short_code and paste_id are mandatory for fast direct retrieval. Foreign keys such as user_id are often indexed to support joins or listing user-owned objects. Frequently queried columns in WHERE clauses should be indexed; however, think about index selectivity and maintenance cost. Partial or filtered indexes are helpful when you only care about a subset of rows, for example indexing expires_at only when it is non-null and status is active. This reduces index size and speeds queries that find expired items for cleanup. A misconception is to index low-selectivity columns like a boolean flag without considering whether the index will be used. Example: an index on access_control may not help if most rows are public. When describing indexes in design interviews, explain the read and write trade-offs and how index choices support specific access patterns like redirect performance or cleanup jobs. Indexing Strategies means index fields you query frequently and consider partial indexes to reduce size and support maintenance jobs.. screens.title: Design a NoSQL Paste Document
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to design a single document structure for Pastebin in a document database like MongoDB. The document should include pasteId, content, syntaxHighlightingLanguage, createdAt, expiresAt, accessControl, passwordHash, userId, and viewCount. Use pasteId as the document key for fast retrieval. screens.title: Choosing SQL, NoSQL, or Hybrid
screens.narratorSegment: When asked to choose a storage approach, explain decisions in terms of the CAP trade-offs and concrete service requirements. If you need strict transactions, complex joins, or strong consistency for metadata, prefer S Q L. If you need flexible schema, horizontal scaling for variable documents, or simple key-value access, prefer NoSQL. Most production systems use a hybrid: store authoritative metadata in S Q L, use a NoSQL key-value store for hot reads, and object storage for heavy binary content. In an interview, state the access patterns, expected read/write ratio, and size distribution upfront. For example, if redirects are ten times more frequent than writes and must be sub-50ms, propose a cache fronted by a durable store. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to design practical data models for two common services: a URL shortener and a Pastebin. We'll define the fields you must store, pick appropriate data types, and reason about which database style makes sense given the access pattern. You will see concrete S Q L table definitions for both services, and we will contrast those with NoSQL and object storage approaches. This matters because good data design makes retrieval fast, storage efficient, and growth predictable. For example, a redirect request depends on a single fast lookup by short code, while paste retrieval may involve very large content blobs that are expensive to keep inside a relational row. We'll also cover indexing strategies, common mistakes like not planning for access patterns, and secure handling of private data such as password hashes. By the end you should be able to choose a primary key, pick sensible types, and recommend when to cache, index, or offload content. Keep in mind the core idea: model data around how it will be read and updated at scale.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to design data schemas for both a URL shortener and a Pastebin service. That means selecting primary keys, choosing field types for variable-length data, and deciding what should be nullable. You will also identify which database model — relational or non-relational — matches a given access pattern. For example, when redirect latency matters and lookups are simple key-to-value, a key-value store or a cached mapping is often the best fit. When paste contents vary greatly in size, a document store or object storage reference is preferable. You will also assess indexing strategies: which columns must be indexed to support fast queries and which can remain unindexed to reduce overhead. Finally, you will identify security constraints such as storing password hashes rather than plaintext, and plan for growth by choosing fields and indexes that scale. These skills let you build efficient, maintainable storage for both services.

Now let’s translate objectives into actions you can perform in an interview or design doc. First, define the ShortenedURL table with a primary key short_code and choose a type that supports six to eight alphanumeric characters. Second, specify the Paste schema and decide whether content stays in the database or files are stored in object storage. Third, design indexes that make the common queries fast — for example, a primary key index on short_code and a filtered index on non-null expires_at for cleanup tasks. Fourth, propose a hybrid storage plan: use a relational database for metadata, a key-value cache for hot redirect lookups, and object storage for very large paste content. Each of these actions shows you understand the trade-offs between consistency, latency, and cost. Practice explaining the rationale: when you prefer ACID transactions and when you prefer horizontal scalability. This applied perspective helps you defend your choices during a system design interview.

A ShortenedURL entity maps a short_code to an original_url and carries metadata used by the service. The short_code must be unique and indexed because redirects are high-volume lookups. Use a VARCHAR sized for six to eight alphanumeric characters to keep keys compact. The original_url should be a TEXT or a large VARCHAR so very long destinations are supported. created_at and expires_at timestamps let you audit and expire entries. A user_id links a short URL to its owner when user accounts exist; treat that as nullable if anonymous creation is allowed. click_count is an often-updated counter and can be stored as a big integer; for very high write rates consider incrementing in a cache and persisting periodically. status as an ENUM helps manage states like active, expired, or disabled. One common misconception is to treat all fields the same: hot key fields like short_code need tight indexing and fast reads, while metadata can be updated less aggressively. Example: when a redirect arrives you only need short_code to original_url; avoid fetching large user metadata during that path. Takeaway: model fields around their runtime use and rate of access.

Understanding access patterns is the practical heart of data model design. For a URL shortener the write path is usually: generate a short_code and insert a new record with original_url and metadata. Reads are extremely frequent: each redirect needs a fast lookup by short_code. Updates are common for click_count increments and occasional status changes. Deletes happen in batch for expired or disabled URLs. Because reads vastly outnumber writes, prioritize read latency: make the short_code lookup as cheap as possible by using a primary key index or a key-value cache. A typical optimization is to store short_code → original_url in a key-value store like Redis for the redirect service and persist metadata to a relational database asynchronously. A misconception is to over-index every column; that can slow writes and inflate storage. Example: only index user_id if you support queries like "list my short URLs." For cleanup, a partial index on expires_at where expires_at IS NOT NULL AND status = 'active' helps the background job find candidates quickly. Question: if read volume spikes, which layer should you scale first — cache or primary store?

A Paste entity stores textual content along with metadata that controls access and lifecycle. Core fields include paste_id as a unique identifier and content as a TEXT or BLOB depending on variability. syntax_highlighting_language is optional but useful for rendering. created_at and expires_at manage lifecycle. access_control distinguishes public, unlisted, and private pastes. If private pastes require a password, never store it in plain text; store a password_hash produced by a strong hashing algorithm such as bcrypt. user_id links pastes to accounts when applicable. view_count tracks reads and can be incremented similarly to click_count. A common mistake is to keep raw passwords or to place very large content directly into transactional hot tables without considering performance. Example: a 5 MB paste stored as a TEXT column can bloat backups and slow queries. Consider storing only metadata in the database and the content in object storage, with a reference in the record. This keeps the metadata fast to scan and the large data in a service designed for big objects. Paste — Core Fields and Security means keep sensitive authentication material hashed and consider external storage for large content to preserve database performance.. In practical terms, essential metadata, content handling, and protecting private pastes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Here is a practical S Q L schema that captures the paste metadata while leaving options for content storage. The paste_id is the primary key for fast lookup. content is declared as TEXT, which is acceptable for moderate sizes, but if you expect megabyte-level pastes you should consider object storage and store a reference instead. We include syntax_highlighting_language, created_at, expires_at, access_control, password_hash, user_id, and view_count. Indexes include user_id when you need to query a user's pastes and a conditional index on expires_at to accelerate cleanup jobs. An important misconception to avoid is assuming that indexing expires_at unconditionally will always help; indexing only active expiration values reduces index bloat. Concrete example: a cleanup job that finds all active pastes with expires_at < now will benefit from a partial index on expires_at where expires_at IS NOT NULL. When explaining this schema in an interview, highlight how each index supports an access pattern and how content storage decisions reduce operational overhead. Example SQL Schema for Pastebin means use a metadata-first sql table and consider partial indexes for lifecycle queries; offload content when sizes grow large.. In practical terms, a concrete table definition and index hints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between S Q L and NoSQL depends on your requirements. For a URL shortener a relational database gives you strong consistency, transactional guarantees, and easy joins if you link URLs to users or billing records. It is a good fit when you need complex queries or strong integrity. A NoSQL key-value store, however, excels at the main redirect path: an extremely fast lookup by short_code with horizontal scalability and low latency. Many teams use a hybrid approach: store authoritative metadata in S Q L for correctness and auditability, while using a key-value cache for the redirect hot path. A common misconception is that NoSQL always means weaker correctness; actually, many NoSQL systems offer tunable consistency and can be perfectly safe when you design around eventual consistency. Example: place short_code → original_url pairs into Redis with a TTL for hot entries and persist authoritative rows to PostgreSQL. In an interview, explain the trade-offs and justify caching based on read volume and latency needs. SQL vs NoSQL: URL Shortener means use sql for integrity and complex queries; use nosql key-value for extremely low-latency hot lookups; hybrid solutions combine strengths.. In practical terms, when to prefer a key-value store or a relational table. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Pastebin has different load characteristics from a URL shortener. Writes create potentially large documents at insert time. Reads fetch content and metadata by paste_id. Updates are usually limited to view_count increments or metadata changes. Deletes happen for expired pastes. Because content size varies widely, the main design question is where to store content: inside the database as TEXT or externally in object storage. If you store in the DB, large content increases row size and can slow scans, backups, and memory usage. If you offload content, the database stores a lightweight reference and metadata; the application fetches the object storage content when needed. A misconception is thinking object storage introduces unacceptable latency — in practice, object stores are optimized for large payloads and can be cached at the CDN layer. A hybrid architecture often gives the best balance between performance and correctness. For the redirect service, keep an authoritative S Q L or NoSQL store for durability and auditing, and layer a key-value cache to answer most redirect requests with minimal latency. For Pastebin, keep metadata in the database and place large content in object storage; use a CDN for frequently accessed large pastes. The pattern is: cache for low-latency reads, database for authoritative metadata and transactions, and object storage for heavy payloads. An important misconception is thinking caches replace databases — they don't. Caches are ephemeral and must be refreshed from the authoritative store on miss. For pastes, the app reads DB metadata, then fetches content from object storage using the stored reference or serves from CDN. Many design mistakes come from not aligning schema choices with access patterns. First, not indexing the short_code is a fatal error for a redirect service: it makes every redirect scan the table. Second, over-normalization can cause excessive joins and hurt latency; under-normalization can cause redundancy and update anomalies. Strike a balance based on expected queries. Third, storing plaintext passwords for private pastes is a security vulnerability; always store a strong hash. Fourth, putting very large content inside transactional tables without offloading to object storage will bloat backups and increase memory pressure. Fifth, indexing every column without thought increases write latency and storage. Example: adding an index on a rarely queried metadata column creates write overhead for every insert. When you describe your design, be explicit about why you indexed specific columns and how that supports a concrete access pattern. Finally, plan for growth: choose flexible types and avoid fixed-size VARCHAR that may overflow in the future. Indexing is key to query performance, but indexes also carry cost. Primary keys on short_code and paste_id are mandatory for fast direct retrieval. Foreign keys such as user_id are often indexed to support joins or listing user-owned objects. Frequently queried columns in WHERE clauses should be indexed; however, think about index selectivity and maintenance cost. Partial or filtered indexes are helpful when you only care about a subset of rows, for example indexing expires_at only when it is non-null and status is active. This reduces index size and speeds queries that find expired items for cleanup. A misconception is to index low-selectivity columns like a boolean flag without considering whether the index will be used. Example: an index on access_control may not help if most rows are public. When asked to choose a storage approach, explain decisions in terms of the CAP trade-offs and concrete service requirements. If you need strict transactions, complex joins, or strong consistency for metadata, prefer S Q L. If you need flexible schema, horizontal scaling for variable documents, or simple key-value access, prefer NoSQL. Most production systems use a hybrid: store authoritative metadata in S Q L, use a NoSQL key-value store for hot reads, and object storage for heavy binary content.
